domain.title: Databases
domain.summary: Modeling, querying, and changing persistent data correctly and efficiently, including under concurrency and schema change.

concepts.title: Relational modeling
concepts.summary: Representing entities and their relationships as tables and rows so data stays consistent and queryable.
learningObjectives: Model one-to-many and many-to-many relationships as tables
Explain the tradeoff between normalization and duplication
Evaluate whether a JSON column is hiding data that should be relational
recognitionSignals: new tables or models, or new relations between them, added to a schema
join tables or many-to-many relation declarations
JSON/JSONB or document-style columns holding structured or list data
delimited strings stored in a single column to represent a list
the same field copied onto multiple tables
misconceptionPatterns: Believing a comma-separated string column is an adequate substitute for a related table
Believing full normalization is always best regardless of access patterns
Believing a JSON column costs nothing compared with real columns and relations, despite losing types, constraints, and efficient filtering

concepts.title: Keys and constraints
concepts.summary: Primary keys, foreign keys, unique, and check constraints let the database enforce invariants that application code can miss.

related.boundary: Duplicate deliveries of the same request or message map there; uniqueness a constraint can enforce maps here.
Read-modify-write of existing row values maps there.

learningObjectives: Explain what each constraint type guarantees
Identify invariants enforced only in application code that race under concurrency
Predict the effect of ON DELETE behaviors on related rows
recognitionSignals: PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, or REFERENCES clauses
ORM unique or foreign-key declarations
ON DELETE CASCADE or SET NULL
an existence check before an insert on a value a UNIQUE constraint could enforce
misconceptionPatterns: Believing a pre-insert existence check guarantees uniqueness without a unique constraint
Believing ON DELETE CASCADE removes only the directly referencing rows, when it follows every cascading relationship recursively
Believing a natural value such as an email or username will never change and is therefore safe as a primary key or foreign-key target
Believing a UNIQUE constraint on a nullable column prevents multiple rows with NULL in that column

concepts.title: Joins
concepts.summary: Combining rows from related tables in one query, and understanding how join type changes which rows appear.
learningObjectives: Predict the rows returned by inner versus left joins
Identify row multiplication from joining one-to-many relationships
Replace an N+1 query pattern with a join or batched query
recognitionSignals: JOIN clauses or ORM include/with relations
queries executed per item in a loop
DISTINCT added to hide duplicate rows
aggregations over joined tables
misconceptionPatterns: Believing a LEFT JOIN returns exactly one row per row of the left table
Believing a filter on the right-hand table behaves the same in WHERE as in the ON clause of a LEFT JOIN
Believing DISTINCT is a correct fix for duplicate rows caused by joining a one-to-many relationship
Assuming loading ORM relations for a list issues a single query

concepts.title: Indexes
concepts.summary: Auxiliary structures, usually B-trees, that make certain lookups fast at the cost of write overhead and storage.
learningObjectives: Explain how an index turns a table scan into a tree lookup
Predict whether a composite index can serve a given WHERE and ORDER BY
Evaluate the write and locking costs of adding an index to a large table
recognitionSignals: CREATE INDEX statements or ORM index declarations
composite or partial indexes
queries filtering or sorting on unindexed columns
migrations that add indexes to existing tables
misconceptionPatterns: Believing adding indexes is free because they only speed up reads
Believing a composite index on (a, b) can generally serve a query that filters or sorts only on b
Believing CREATE INDEX on a live table is non-blocking, when in Postgres a plain build blocks writes until it finishes (CONCURRENTLY avoids this but cannot run inside a transaction block)
Believing that declaring a foreign key automatically indexes the referencing column (Postgres does not; MySQL InnoDB does)

concepts.title: Transactions
concepts.summary: Grouping several reads and writes so they commit together or not at all, keeping data consistent when something fails midway.
learningObjectives: Identify multi-step writes that leave inconsistent data if interrupted
Explain atomicity and what a rollback undoes
Recognize side effects such as emails or HTTP calls that a transaction cannot roll back
recognitionSignals: BEGIN/COMMIT or db.transaction(...) blocks
several related inserts or updates in one handler
external API calls between database writes
manual compensation or cleanup code after failures
misconceptionPatterns: Believing consecutive write statements in one request handler are atomic without an explicit transaction
Believing a rollback also undoes emails, HTTP calls, or queue messages sent inside the transaction
Believing it is harmless to hold a transaction open across slow network calls, when it keeps locks and a pooled connection for the whole duration
Believing every query inside a transaction callback participates in the transaction, even when it uses the global client instead of the transaction handle

concepts.title: Isolation and concurrent writes
concepts.summary: Isolation levels and row locks determine what concurrent transactions can see and overwrite.
learningObjectives: Explain lost updates and write skew with a concrete interleaving
Predict what a second statement in the same transaction sees under READ COMMITTED versus REPEATABLE READ after a concurrent commit
Compare atomic conditional updates, optimistic version checks, SELECT FOR UPDATE, and serializable isolation with retries
Defend a concurrency-control choice for a specific read-modify-write workflow
recognitionSignals: read-modify-write of existing row values (balances, counters, stock) across separate statements
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or version columns
isolation level configuration
retry-on-serialization-failure logic
misconceptionPatterns: Believing wrapping a read-modify-write in a transaction prevents lost updates at the default isolation level
Believing the default isolation level is serializable (Postgres defaults to READ COMMITTED; MySQL InnoDB to REPEATABLE READ)
Believing reading a value into application memory, changing it, and writing it back is as safe as an atomic update such as SET count = count + 1
Believing SELECT ... FOR UPDATE also prevents concurrent inserts of rows that did not exist when it ran
Believing serializable isolation never raises errors, so no retry logic is needed

concepts.title: Schema migrations
concepts.summary: Versioned, ordered schema changes that must run safely against live data and running application code.
learningObjectives: Explain why migrations must be compatible with both old and new application versions during deploys
Identify destructive or long-locking migration steps
Design an expand-and-contract sequence for renaming a column
recognitionSignals: files in a migrations directory
ALTER TABLE, DROP COLUMN, or NOT NULL additions
data backfill scripts
ORM-generated migration SQL
misconceptionPatterns: Believing the migration and the new application code go live at the same instant, so old code never runs against the new schema

Believing a schema change that is logically quick is safe on a busy table, when an ALTER TABLE waiting for its exclusive lock can queue behind a long-running transaction and block all reads and writes on that table
Believing SET NOT NULL or adding a foreign key to a large existing table is a cheap metadata change, when it scans the table while holding a strong lock (NOT VALID then VALIDATE avoids the long lock)
Believing it is safe to edit a migration that has already been applied in another environment
Believing a down migration or deploy rollback restores data removed by dropping a column or table

concepts.title: Query performance
concepts.summary: Reading query plans and access patterns to understand why a query is slow and what will fix it.
learningObjectives: Interpret the main parts of an EXPLAIN plan
Explain why a query that is fast in development is slow in production
Choose between indexing, rewriting, caching, or denormalizing for a slow query
recognitionSignals: EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE output
WHERE clauses that wrap a column in a function or cast, or use LIKE with a leading wildcard
COUNT, aggregation, or ORDER BY over large tables executed on every request
queries without LIMIT over tables that grow with usage
fetching many rows to filter, sort, or aggregate in application code instead of in SQL
misconceptionPatterns: Believing the ORM always generates efficient SQL
Assuming a query's speed on development data predicts its speed at production volume
Believing the planner will use an index whenever one exists on a filtered column
Believing EXPLAIN without ANALYZE reports actual row counts and timings
Believing a cache is the right first fix for a slow query whose plan has not been examined

concepts.title: Database connections and pooling
concepts.summary: Database connections are scarce, stateful server resources; pools and external poolers share a bounded number of them across requests, processes, and serverless instances.

related.boundary: Instance start, freeze, and shutdown behavior maps there; connection counts and pooler semantics map here.
Limiting in-flight application work maps there.

learningObjectives: Explain why the database server limits connections and what each connection costs
Predict total connection demand from pool size multiplied by processes or serverless instances
Identify code that creates a new database client or pool per request instead of reusing one
Compare an in-process pool with an external transaction-mode pooler and name the session features the latter breaks
recognitionSignals: database client or pool constructed inside a request handler or function body
pool size, connection_limit, or max connections settings
connection strings or drivers targeting a connection pooler or serverless database proxy
global singleton caching of a database client to survive hot reload
handling of 'too many connections' or pool acquire timeout errors
misconceptionPatterns: Believing opening a new database connection for each request is cheap
Believing a larger pool always increases throughput
Believing a configured pool size applies to the whole application rather than to each process or serverless instance
Believing session state such as prepared statements, SET parameters, or advisory locks persists between queries behind a transaction-mode pooler
